Patients who have been considered to be at risk of developing en- docarditis include those with:4,7,9 • acquired valvular heart disease • congenital heart disease, including septal defects, tetral- ogy of Fallot, or aortic stenosis • hypertrophic cardiomyopathy • mitral valve prolapse with valvular regurgitation • prosthetic valves or shunts • a history of endocarditis Traditionally, these groups have been subdivided into those at moderate and high risk, but some guidelines no longer make such a distinction. As for treatment, guidelines have been periodically issued to guide the selection of antibacterials for prophylaxis be- fore various procedures in patients at risk.4,7,9-11 Proce- dures that have been thought likely to produce bacteraemia and therefore to require prophylactic treatment include any dental intervention likely to cause bleeding, other oral or upper-respiratory tract operations such as tonsillectomy, certain gastrointestinal procedures such as sclerotherapy for oesophageal varices or biliary-tract surgery, and some urinary-tract surgery.4,7,9 Whether prophylaxis is truly needed before dental procedures is a subject of controver- sy. US guidelines10 recommend antibacterial prophylaxis only for dental procedures that involve manipulation of gingival tissues or periapical region of teeth, or perforation of oral mucosa in patients considered to be at the highest risk of developing adverse outcomes from endocarditis (such as those with a history of infective endocarditis, car- diac valve replacement surgery, or some patients with con- genital heart disease). US guidelines also recommend an- tibacterial prophylaxis for high-risk patients for procedures on respiratory tract or infected skin, skin struc- tures, or musculoskeletal tissue, but do not recommend prophylaxis for genitourinary or gastrointestinal tract pro- cedures. Similar recommendations were made in the UK by the British Society for Antimicrobial Chemotherapy in 20069 but subsequent guidelines issued by NICE11 and adopted by the BNF essentially abolished the requirement for standard antibacterial prophylaxis in any procedure. Antibacterial prophylaxis is aimed mainly at viridans streptococci and HACEK organisms before dental, oral, respiratory, and oesophageal procedures, and at enterococ- ci, Strep. bovis, and the Enterobacteriaceae before gas- trointestinal and genito-urinary procedures.7 Drugs should be given in a regimen that assures adequate blood concen- trations throughout the procedure. They are generally giv- en as a single dose before the procedure, sometimes re- peated about 6 hours later; the oral route is used if possible. •
